title: The caterpillar's crossing
hook: a small creature at the end of a blade of grass never lets go until it has hold of the next one
carry: death is a crossing, carrying what we did
tomorrow: "as is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed"

segments.voice: Yesterday: deep sleep, the falcon folding its wings, held with no inside and no outside. Your line was in deep sleep, the self is still there.
screen: `IN DEEP SLEEP, THE SELF IS STILL THERE.`

segments.voice: Crouch down in a garden and watch a caterpillar climb a blade of grass. At the tip, it doesn't fall off, and it doesn't jump. It stretches its front end out into the air, waving a little, until it touches the next blade. It grips. Only then does it let go of the old one and draw the rest of itself across. Yajnavalkya and King Janaka have walked through waking, dreaming and deep sleep. Now the sage takes the last step, the one everyone takes, and he uses that caterpillar.
screen: `AT THE TIP OF A BLADE OF GRASS.` → `IT REACHES, AND GRIPS.` → `ONLY THEN DOES IT LET GO.`

segments.voice: First he describes the dying, gently. The senses gather around the self, the way a king's officers gather when he's about to travel. Then the tip of the heart lights up, and by that light the self leaves, and the breath and the senses follow. And what goes with it? What it knew, and what it did, and what it had lived. Then the picture. As a caterpillar, coming to the end of a blade of grass, reaches out to another and draws itself across, so the self lays down this body, reaches out to another support and draws itself across. And one more: as a goldsmith hammers a piece of gold into a newer, more beautiful shape, so the self makes itself another form. This is the Hindu teaching of rebirth. Death isn't a fall into nothing. The self lets go of one body and crosses to the next, and what it carries is what it knew and what it did: its karma. You met Krishna's picture in the Gita last year, old clothes laid aside for new; it's the same teaching. It's why Hindu families gather for the last rites, antyeshti, with fire and prayers, and keep making offerings for the one who has gone: many understand it as helping someone across. This week: Gargi's arrows, one truth, the root, the self's light, dreams, deep sleep, and today, the crossing.
screen: `THE SENSES GATHER; THE HEART LIGHTS UP.` · `THE CATERPILLAR REACHES THE NEXT BLADE.` · `REBIRTH, CARRYING KARMA.` · `ANTYESHTI: HELPING SOMEONE ACROSS.` · then, large: `DEATH IS A CROSSING, CARRYING WHAT WE DID.`

segments.voice: At the very end of each out-breath, notice the tiny reach toward the next breath; then let the old breath go, without hurrying it. If thoughts of death come, someone you've lost, or your own, let them be here too. If you pray, name the one you've lost and wish them a safe crossing; if not, just keep breathing, one blade to the next.
Death, as the Brihadaranyaka pictures it: a caterpillar at the tip of a blade of grass, reaching for the next before it lets go.
Your line: death is a crossing, carrying what we did. The gold is still the same gold. Day three hundred eighty-five, done.

howItsDone: Hindu funeral rites, antyeshti, are performed by the family with fire and mantras, and the days that follow include offerings for the departed; passages like this one and Bhagavad Gita 2.22 may be read or recalled at the time of a death.
